note: Plain-language due-diligence on every supplier — the ones in a recommendation and your current suppliers. Serious flags were verified against primary sources (FDA, CCI, courts). Each is a lead to verify before acting, not a final legal conclusion. Full sourced detail: research/supplier-due-diligence.md.

gujarat-ambuja-exports.headline: India's #1 maize processor — financially rock-solid, but profit swings hard.
gujarat-ambuja-exports.verdict: Push the price down — you're overpaying a debt-free market leader. No reason to switch.
findings: Net-debt-free, top-tier AA– credit; ~₹950 cr cash. Low-risk to rely on.
Profit is a commodity spread — one quarter fell 45% year-on-year, then rebounded sharply.
A 2018 pollution complaint led to an NGT closure order at its Sitarganj plant (since stayed).
Governance quirks: ₹40 cr+ promoter pay vs a ~3% dividend on a big cash pile.

sukhjit-corn-products.headline: Healthy, well-run dextrose maker with blue-chip clients.
sukhjit-corn-products.verdict: Cut the price AND stop paying them early — both are safe concessions to reclaim.
findings: A-rated, low debt; clients include Dabur, Nestlé, Mars, Marico.
Margin dip recently cut its grade A+ → A — earnings are cyclical, but the balance sheet is strong.
Runs its bank limits ~93% full, so the early cash you give them is something they value.

sayaji-industries.headline: A suggested dextrose alternative — financially fragile, but recovering.
sayaji-industries.verdict: Use only as a small price-lever second source. Don't move real volume here until the recovery is proven.

flag.label: Financially fragile (recovering)
flag.detail: Still below investment grade (CARE BB+), and its FY25 operating profit was actually negative — held together by promoter cash injections and a ₹73 cr land sale. It is now recovering: the credit outlook moved to Positive (Sep 2026) on a margin recovery. Improving, but not yet a supplier to lean on heavily.

findings: Below investment grade (CARE BB+), slid from BBB+ over three years.
FY25 operating profit was negative; its gum-arabic JV out-earns the whole parent company.
Survival has leaned on promoter loans and asset sales, not operations.

universal-starch-chem-allied.headline: Small, opaque dextrose maker that went dark on its rating agency.
universal-starch-chem-allied.verdict: Push the price; don't grow reliance. The self-chosen opacity is the flag.
findings: Stopped sharing its books (and paying fees) with its rating agency — downgraded to BB for it.
Entered the dextrose business by buying a bank-auctioned distressed plant for ₹17 cr.
Tiny (~₹490 cr revenue), zero dividends despite profits; high-pollution category plant.

geep-industries-india.headline: Your biggest laminate supplier — and a convicted cartelist.
geep-industries-india.verdict: Push the price hard; don't grow reliance. Laminate is a sideline for them, and the conviction + opacity are real flags.

flag.label: Convicted of cartelisation (CCI, 2018)
flag.detail: India's competition regulator (CCI) found GEEP guilty in 2018 of running a price-fixing cartel with Panasonic in dry-cell batteries (penalty ~₹9.6 cr); the guilt finding was upheld on appeal. "GEEP" is the old Geep batteries/torch brand — laminate film is a side business.

findings: A battery/torch/LED company that also converts laminate — packaging is non-core.
Margins compressed from ~8.6% to ~3%; the group's growth story is LED/EV, not laminate.
History of going 'non-cooperating' with its rating agency.

shrinath-roto-pack.headline: A real, pharma-grade laminate alternative — but carrying factory debt.
shrinath-roto-pack.verdict: Bring in as a second source alongside GEEP to push price and build a backup — dual-source, don't hand them everything yet.
findings: Big (57,540 tonnes/yr), pharma-grade; supplies GSK, P&G, Britannia; live US exports.
But cash flow cratered ~80% and free cash is just ₹1.95 cr — tighter than its BBB+ grade suggests.
Credit is hostage to an under-utilised (40–50%), over-budget aluminium-foil plant it guarantees.
One rating agency marked it 'non-cooperating' just before it switched agencies.

tetrapak-india.headline: Rock-solid global supplier you're paying too early.
tetrapak-india.verdict: Stop paying early; push for 30-day terms — they finance their own customers, so they have no basis to make you pay upfront.
findings: Financially dominant MNC; India's largest Tetra Pak plant is near Pune.
The group carries two of the largest antitrust fines in EU and Chinese history (for tying packaging to machines).
The India arm repatriates ~₹300 cr/yr to Sweden — relevant to why you shouldn't be paying early.

gls-films-industries-p.headline: Big laminate capacity, but financially fragile and opaque.
gls-films-industries-p.verdict: Push the price hard; don't increase reliance without fresh financial comfort.

flag.label: Near-insolvency AND a fatal fire at the parent group
flag.detail: A creditor got GLS admitted to insolvency (NCLAT 2025, which called its defence a 'moonshine defence'); the Supreme Court reversed it in 2026. The group did not cover its interest in FY24, and shows 'rating shopping' (two agencies went non-cooperating after FY24 accounts disclosed debt-servicing delays; a third then graded it higher). SEPARATELY, a reactor blast at sister company GLS Speciality Chemicals killed 4 workers (May 2026); the fire-safety officer was arrested and the complaint alleged earlier safety warnings were ignored.

findings: Plenty of capacity (78,800 t/yr, ~50% used) and blue-chip clients (ITC, PepsiCo, Nestlé).
But the combined group didn't cover its interest in FY24 (interest-cover 0.86x, heavily geared).
Flagship revenue fell ~23%; survives on promoter loans and cross-guarantees.

huhtamaki-india.headline: Very strong, pharma-grade laminate maker — the solid alternative.
huhtamaki-india.verdict: Safe to move volume here and use their flat revenue to push price. Just monitor the leadership reset.
findings: Very safe credit (AA–), almost no debt, >₹400 cr cash, backed by a Finnish parent.
Pharma-grade (makes pharma tube laminates); 90-year operating history.
Watch-item: the MD and CFO both resigned within ~3 months (late 2025).

uflex.headline: India's largest flexible-packaging firm — capable, but with governance & debt flags.
uflex.verdict: Use as a price benchmark only; don't concentrate volume. The chairman's conviction and the leverage are the flags.

flag.label: Chairman convicted in a corruption case
flag.detail: Founder-chairman Ashok Chaturvedi was convicted by a CBI court (2010) in the Noida land-allotment scam and jailed. Separately, the company is heavily indebted (net-debt/EBITDA 4.25x, credit outlook cut to Negative). Note: a 2023 tax-raid headline actually collapsed at the tax tribunal in 2026.

findings: Large and technically capable — a good lever to push other laminate prices down.
Heavily indebted; credit outlook recently cut to Negative; thin ~2% margins.
Trades at ~0.4x book — the market heavily discounts it.

silk-polypack.headline: Not a real supplier — a single one-off purchase.
silk-polypack.verdict: Drop from alternatives. FDC's own records show just one ₹7,775 / 31 kg laminate receipt (Mar 2026).
findings: One purchase ever in FDC's SAP records — ₹7,775, 31 kg of laminate (27 Mar 2026).
No company registry or web footprint, because there's effectively nothing there.

chemco-plastic-industries.headline: Strong, pharma-grade bottle maker — 'old stock' is just how they run.
chemco-plastic-industries.verdict: Keep them — but add a 'freshest-first / max-age-at-dispatch' clause for ORS shelf life.
findings: Strong credit (A+), revenue ~₹939 cr, pharma clients (Cipla, J&J).
The 'old stock' you flagged is their deliberate ~125-day inventory model, not distress.
Built a >1-billion-bottle/yr food-grade recycled-PET plant; a ₹1,500 cr IPO is talked about (no filing yet).

cincorp-international.headline: A genuine pharma-bottle maker — just pin down the exact legal entity.
cincorp-international.verdict: Use the overpay data to negotiate; confirm the exact invoicing entity from a GST invoice.
findings: Confirmed a real manufacturer (Noida) of HDPE/LDPE/PP pharma bottles — not a middleman.
FDC's own records show 121 deliveries of bottles + caps to your Baddi plant.
The public company-registry match is murky, so verify the exact legal entity.

pik-plastics.headline: A real but tiny Surat bottle maker — unaudited.
pik-plastics.verdict: Fine for price leverage now; don't move volume without an on-site audit + documents.
findings: A real one-owner firm (Surat) with a Vapi factory and a Haridwar pharma-belt branch.
No audited accounts, capacity figures or pharma certificates could be verified.

premier-plastic.headline: A micro one-owner plastics shop — weakest pharma fit.
premier-plastic.verdict: Confirm exactly which 'Premier' invoices FDC (get the GST number), then audit before any volume move.
findings: The real supplier is a tiny Vasai proprietorship — NOT the healthy listed 'Premier Polyfilm' (that's a vinyl-flooring company).
Its catalogue is general plastics (jars, tablet tubes, even scarf hangers) — thin pharma-bottle evidence.

mars-plastics.headline: A small Punjab partnership — best pharma product-fit of the tiny ones.
mars-plastics.verdict: Fine for price leverage; audit before moving meaningful volume.
findings: Makes exactly the right products (dry-syrup, eye-drop, nasal bottles) — good fit.
But a ₹5–25 cr partnership with no audited accounts or confirmed pharma certs.

berry-global-india.headline: Backed by a global giant (Amcor) — but confirm they make your bottle.
berry-global-india.verdict: Safe to move to on parent strength — first confirm the India plant makes your exact ORS bottle SKU.
findings: Parent is now Amcor (~$13bn, investment-grade) after an Apr-2025 acquisition — rock-solid.
But the India legal entity is tiny and loss-making; its Bangalore site makes drug-delivery devices (inhalers/droppers), maybe not plain bottles.
Amcor is mid-restructuring (US plant closures so far).

suraj-blow-plast.headline: A real small bottle maker — just has no web footprint.
suraj-blow-plast.verdict: Use as leverage; audit before bigger volume.
findings: FDC's records confirm 38 deliveries of amber PET pharma bottles to Aurangabad (~₹4.95/pc).
Genuine supplier; no public registry/web presence, so no independent financials to check.

tpac-packaging-india.headline: Healthy, A-rated bottle maker backed by a Thai group.
tpac-packaging-india.verdict: Push the price, ideally with a resin-cost-linked clause. Safe to keep or grow.
findings: A-rated, ~₹822 cr revenue, pharma-capable, multiple India plants.
Watch-items: profit dipped ~31% last year, and it leans ~85–90% on a single supplier of its own.

kilitch-healthcare-india.headline: Flagged for old stock — and the most serious finding of the set.
kilitch-healthcare-india.verdict: Treat as elevated-risk. Require their FDA remediation evidence and re-qualify them, or move the business.

flag.label: US FDA found fabricated lab data + import ban
flag.detail: FDA Warning Letter (28 Mar 2024) found it is their 'routine practice to fabricate results for samples that were never taken', plus insanitary conditions. On FDA Import Alert 66-40 since Oct 2023; the maker behind the 2023 US store-brand eye-drop recall. For a pharma buyer, fabricated QC data undermines trust in all their test paperwork. (This is the unlisted Kilitch Healthcare, not the clean listed Kilitch Drugs.)

findings: A pharma contract-manufacturer — likely supplies FDC filled/finished goods, not empty bottles.
Formerly named 'NBZ Pharma'; FY25 profit fell ~44% after the US import ban.
The ~211-day-old stock is especially concerning given the data-integrity findings.

empire-industries-virum-glass.headline: Your amber glass-bottle maker — a steady niche unit of a cash-rich Mumbai group.
empire-industries-virum-glass.verdict: Keep — a long-established, low-continuity-risk supplier. Just confirm the glass type (Type I vs III) suits your product.
findings: Solid credit (A-/A), cash-rich and low-geared; the group's real profit engine is property rentals.
Vikhroli plant makes molded amber pharma glass; clients include GSK, Pfizer, Merck, Cipla.
Glass is a small, non-core division of the listed Empire Industries — thin public disclosure on the unit itself.

bprex-pharma-packaging-india-p.headline: A cGMP pharma-packaging maker built for eye-drops — now part of Amcor.
bprex-pharma-packaging-india-p.verdict: Keep — a well-capitalised, low-risk MNC vendor. Confirm which entity (legacy Bprex vs Berry Global India) actually invoices you.
findings: Strong lineage: Truepack → Rexam → Berry → Amcor (2025); the parent is investment-grade.
Bangalore cGMP clean-room makes ophthalmic dropper bottles — a strong fit for FDC's eye-drops.
Shares the same Bangalore address and directors as Berry Global India (same Amcor group).

pgp-glass.headline: A world-scale glass leader (ex-Piramal Glass) — very capable, but its ownership is changing hands.
pgp-glass.verdict: Keep; monitor the Blackstone IPO / sale and the March-2026 refinancing — an owner change could shift focus off low-margin domestic pharma.

flag.label: Ownership in flux
flag.detail: 100% owned by Blackstone (since 2020), which is now running a parallel IPO (~$4bn aspiration) AND trade-sale talks (Brookfield ~$1.3–1.5bn), plus a ₹2,597 cr loan due March 2026 that is being refinanced (Blackstone backstop). Pharma is only ~21% of its sales — ~77% is luxury cosmetics & spirits — so an ownership change could move priorities away from your low-margin domestic pharma glass.

findings: Very capable: A+ credit, ~₹4,216 cr revenue, ~33% margins; the Type-I pharma-glass leader.
But pharma is a minority of its book — most of it is luxury cosmetics and spirits bottles.
Strong ESG record (EcoVadis Platinum, CDP 'A'); zero fatalities FY25.

sources.label: CARE, Dec 2025; PGP FY25 annual report

rachana-plastics.headline: A one-man Mumbai maker of caps and measuring cups — clean record, but tiny and opaque.
rachana-plastics.verdict: Low-stakes closure/cup supplier. Pin the exact GST entity and check food-grade (FSSAI) compliance.
findings: Almost certainly a sole proprietorship (Jignesh Gandhi) — key-person risk.
Makes flip-off seals, screw caps, child-resistant caps and 5/15/250 ml measuring cups — ORS-relevant.
No public financials and no review footprint; clean record, but zero financial transparency.

abhinav-speciality-foods-llp.headline: A tiny, opaque Mumbai family LLP — what it actually supplies FDC isn't publicly clear.
abhinav-speciality-foods-llp.verdict: Get its FSSAI licence, the exact product spec / COA and GST number, and clarify the link to the adjacent Ayurvedic business.
findings: Very small (~₹4 cr revenue) and leveraged — its debt is roughly the size of its whole balance sheet.
Office in Andheri with no visible factory; the exact ingredient supplied is undiscoverable publicly.
Adjacent to an Ayurvedic business (Abhinav Healthcare) — the highest information-risk of the whole set.

triveni-polymers.headline: The standout 'small' vendor — actually a wholly-owned arm of Germany's Gerresheimer.
triveni-polymers.verdict: The strongest and lowest-risk of your small vendors — a tier-1 global player. Keep, and you could safely grow it.
findings: 100% owned by Gerresheimer AG (German pharma-packaging MNC); branded 'Gerresheimer Kundli'.
USFDA-DMF-certified (the first Indian firm for plastic pharma containers); ISO / USP / EP compliant.
Clean-room plants at Kundli + Kosamba; capacity nearly doubled since 2012. Great Place To Work certified.

scorpion-containers.headline: Named like a packaging maker — but the evidence points to a logistics / freight firm.
scorpion-containers.verdict: Confirm what they actually supply you (bottles vs transport) before treating them as a packaging vendor.

flag.label: May not be a packaging maker at all
flag.detail: Despite the 'Containers' name, the trail — courier GST codes, 10+ multi-state registrations, and the 'Scorpion Express' pan-India 3PL logistics group — points to freight / transport, not manufacturing. Only one thin packaging listing (PET bottles / HDPE jars) exists. The FDC relationship may well be transport, not bottles.

findings: Tiny (paid-up under ₹1 cr); no credit rating, no public financials, no verifiable plant or capacity.
Run by the Singh family, who also operate the Scorpion Express logistics group.
The 'packaging supplier' premise is only weakly supported by the public record.
